procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The NCDRC order was challenged before the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court heard Civil Appeal No. 3975 of 2018, C.A. No.4847 of 2018 and 6917 of 2023 and disposed of the appeals.

directions: The judgment awarding Rs. 6,11,638/- as compensation @ 9% simple interest p.a. on account of medical negligence committed by the single act of performing the aforesaid ‘NI’ procedure, is found to be erroneous and is set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether there was a breach of duty of care, with respect to the ‘NI’ procedure performed on 13.05.2004. In case a breach did occur, speciﬁ c breach of responsibility of the concerned person shall have to be established;

facts: On 13.05.2004, a patient underwent an 'NI' procedure to replace an existing Tracheostomy Tube ('TT').
This was done after a bronchoscopy report indicated that the patient's airways and trachea were normal.
After the 'TT' was removed (decannulated), the patient developed a 'stridor' (an abnormal, high-pitched breathing sound), which was an unexpected complication.
In response to the stridor, the medical team, led by Dr. Rajesh Swarnakar, opted for the 'NI' procedure as a temporary, alternative course of treatment.
An independent medical report from the RML Hospital Committee did not attribute any negligence to the hospital or doctors regarding the procedure.
law: To establish medical negligence, there must be: 1) a duty of care, 2) a breach of that duty, and 3) resulting harm from the breach.
A medical practitioner is only liable for negligence if their conduct falls below the standards of a reasonably competent practitioner.
Adopting an alternative, accepted medical course of action does not, in itself, amount to negligence.
A treatment that does not yield the desired result is not automatically considered negligent.
application: The Court found that the decision to perform the 'NI' procedure was not a negligent act but a considered medical judgment in response to an unforeseen complication (the stridor).
The Court determined that the 'NI' procedure was an 'accepted medical course of action' and there was no evidence to show it was outdated or constituted poor medical practice.
The Court relied on the principle that choosing an alternative treatment plan, especially when faced with an unexpected development, is not a breach of duty.
The Court also gave weight to the RML Hospital Committee Report, noting that if the procedure had been negligent, the expert committee would likely have mentioned it, but it made no such observation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the claim, concluding that there was no breach of the duty of care. The 'NI' procedure was a reasonable and accepted medical response to an unexpected complication that arose during treatment, and therefore, the charge of negligence was not proved.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there was a breach of duty of care, with respect to the ‘NI’ procedure performed on 13.05.2004. In case a breach did occur, speciﬁ c breach of responsibility of the concerned person shall have to be established;
appellant_arguments: The appellants (the doctors and the hospital) argued that they were not medically negligent. They contended that just because a chosen line of treatment does not achieve the desired result, it does not automatically amount to negligence, provided the course of action was a recognized and sound medical practice. They likely argued that the 'NI' procedure, even if it entailed a higher risk, was a valid medical option selected after due consideration and deliberation, and was not an obsolete or discarded practice.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (Mrs. Sunita) argued that the doctors and the hospital were negligent and breached their duty of care in performing the 'NI' procedure.

cases.case_name: Jacob Mathew vs. State of Punjab
cases.principle: A doctor cannot be held liable for negligence just because they opt for a particular line of treatment that does not achieve the desired result, provided the course of action was recognized as a sound and relevant medical practice and was not of a discarded or obsolete category.

cases.principle: A doctor cannot be held liable for negligence just because they opt for a particular line of treatment that does not achieve the desired result, provided the course of action was recognized as a sound and relevant medical practice and was not of a discarded or obsolete category.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A doctor is not liable for negligence if they choose a line of treatment that fails, provided the chosen course of action is recognized as a sound and current medical practice, even if other professionals would have chosen differently or the procedure involved higher risk. To establish negligence, a complainant must meet a higher burden of proof, demonstrating that the doctor either did not possess the requisite skill they professed, or did not exercise their possessed skill with the reasonable competence of an ordinary practitioner.
obiter: The higher threshold for medical negligence is intended to ensure doctors can focus on treatment decisions in high-risk situations without being concerned about potential persecution or harassment.

Due to the unique circumstances of individual cases and constant advancements in medicine, it is natural for different and even contesting opinions to exist regarding the appropriate line of treatment.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A doctor cannot be held liable for negligence just because a chosen line of treatment does not achieve the desired result. This holds true even if the procedure entailed a higher risk, provided that the course of action was a recognized, sound, and relevant medical practice, and not a discarded or obsolete one. A professional who takes a higher element of risk, looking to the gravity of the illness to redeem the patient, may not be found negligent if the treatment does not yield the desired result.
legal_tests_applied: The essential components of negligence are three: ‘duty’, ‘breach’, and ‘resulting damage’.

A professional may be held liable for negligence if: either he was not possessed of the requisite skill which he professed to have possessed, or he did not exercise, with reasonable competence in the given case, the skill which he did possess.
In the realm of diagnosis and treatment, there is scope for genuine difference of opinion, and a doctor is not negligent merely because his conclusion differs from that of another professional.

To hold a medical practitioner liable for negligence, a higher threshold limit must be met, and the complainant must be able to prove a breach of duty and the subsequent injury being attributable to that breach.
Doctors, in turn, need to establish that they had followed reasonable standards of medical practice.
policy_considerations: It is the 'bounden duty and obligation of the civil society to ensure that the medical professionals are not unnecessarily harassed or humiliated so that they can perform their professional duties without fear and apprehension.'

A higher threshold for proving medical negligence is necessary 'to ensure that these doctors are focused on deciding the best course of treatment as per their assessment rather than being concerned about possible persecution or harassment that they may be subjected to in high-risk medical situations.'
